tldr: Nvidia confirms a $12.93 billion deal for Hugging Face, the open-model hub its own chip rivals depend on.
US forces destroy or disable three Iranian oil tankers after Iran fires ballistic missiles at two Navy warships.
August payrolls came in at 162,000 against a 53,000 forecast, pushing traders toward betting on a Fed rate hike.
FDA approves camizestrant, the first cancer drug cleared on the basis of a blood test rather than a scan showing growth.
Witkoff and Kushner meet Putin for three hours in Moscow and head to Kyiv with a proposal to end the war.
OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra is the first model it rates "Critical" for cyber capability; its headline benchmark is disputed.
Ionis wins approval for Zanvastro, the first treatment ever for Alexander disease.
The Justice Department tells a federal court that training AI on copyrighted work is fair use.
The FBI investigates a dark-web service that offered scans of 153 million driver's licenses.
A judge curbs work on Trump's $100 million arch, days after the Chief Justice called the companion ballroom "likely unlawful."

items.headline: Nvidia buys Hugging Face, the neutral hub of open-model AI, for $12.93 billion
items.body: Nvidia confirmed on September 3 that it will acquire Hugging Face for about $12.93 billion, disclosing the agreement in an SEC filing dated September 2. The price includes an equity retention pool of up to $1 billion for Hugging Face staff who join. The platform is used by more than 18 million developers hosting over 3 million models, and by more than 200,000 companies. CEO Jensen Huang said Hugging Face "will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem" and that "Nvidia compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face." The deal is Nvidia's second-largest after roughly $20 billion for Groq assets last year, and is expected to close in the first half of 2027 pending regulatory clearance in the US, EU and likely the UK.
items.plain: Hugging Face is the shared library where AI researchers publish and download the free, downloadable models that anyone can run - think of it as the app store for open AI, except it is not owned by any chipmaker. Nvidia makes the chips almost all of those models are trained on, including for its competitors. Buying the library means the dominant supplier now owns the shelf its rivals' products sit on. Nvidia says nothing will change; that is exactly what regulators will spend the next year testing.
items.why: Antitrust review of vertical AI deals has mostly been theoretical until now, and this one puts a chip monopoly and a distribution chokepoint in the same company for regulators to rule on.

items.headline: US destroys or disables three Iranian tankers after missiles are fired at two Navy warships
items.body: US Central Command said that on Saturday, September 5, American aircraft and drones permanently disabled the crude carriers M/T Downy off Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask, and destroyed the unladen M/T Kylo in the Gulf of Oman after directing its crew to abandon ship. The strikes followed Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps ballistic missile launches at a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer, which evaded the attacks; no American personnel were hurt. CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said: "If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost - taking out three of yours." US officials described it as a new "tanker for tanker" policy approved by President Trump. Brent crude closed Friday near $96 a barrel, up about 9% on the week.
items.plain: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow sea passage that roughly a fifth of the world's oil moves through, and Iran sits along one side of it. Iran funds armed groups partly by selling oil from a "shadow fleet" of tankers that hide their ownership. Rather than bomb Iranian territory and risk a wider war, the US is now sinking the money-making ships instead - trading military escalation for economic pain. The catch is that attacking tankers in the world's most important oil lane is itself what pushes oil prices up.
items.why: Targeting the revenue fleet instead of Iranian soil is a deliberate attempt to punish without invading, which means this exchange can continue indefinitely rather than resolving.

items.headline: Hiring triples the forecast and Wall Street starts pricing in a rate hike
items.body: US nonfarm payrolls rose 162,000 in August, against a consensus of 53,000, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. Unemployment held at 4.1%; average hourly earnings rose 0.3% on the month and 3.1% on the year. It was the strongest monthly gain since March. Bars and restaurants led hiring while information-sector employment fell. Fed funds futures moved sharply toward a rate increase at the September 15-16 meeting: CME FedWatch pricing cited by CNBC put the odds near 58%, up from 49.4% a day earlier, while other reports put them above 60%. The two-year Treasury yield rose to about 4.37%, its highest since January 2025. The S&P 500 fell 0.38% to 7,718.60 and the Dow lost 0.51% to 53,414.25.
items.plain: The Federal Reserve sets the interest rate that ripples through mortgages, car loans and credit cards. It raises that rate when the economy runs hot enough to push prices up, and cuts it when hiring stalls. Forecasters expected a weak August, which would have argued for cuts. Instead employers added three times as many jobs as predicted, and traders flipped to betting on a hike. The odd detail: the jobs came from restaurants and bars, while information-sector work shrank, which some analysts attribute to AI displacing those roles.
items.why: A hike would put the Fed in the position of tightening into an economy where oil is climbing on a shooting war, compounding a price shock rather than cushioning it.

items.headline: FDA clears the first cancer drug approved on a blood test rather than a scan
items.body: On September 4 the FDA granted accelerated approval to camizestrant, sold as Etcamah by AstraZeneca, combined with a CDK4/6 inhibitor for hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer once an ESR1 mutation is detected in the blood during existing therapy. It is the first cancer therapy approved on the basis of a resistance mutation found in circulating tumor DNA before any scan shows the disease growing. In the SERENA-6 trial, 3,256 patients were screened and 315 randomized; median progression-free survival was 16.0 months versus 9.2 months on continued aromatase inhibitor therapy, a hazard ratio of 0.44. The FDA simultaneously authorized Guardant360 CDx as the companion blood test.
items.plain: Tumors evolve. A breast cancer controlled by one drug will often acquire a mutation called ESR1 that makes that drug stop working - and doctors normally only find out months later, when a scan shows the tumor growing again. Tumors shed fragments of their DNA into the bloodstream, so a blood test can spot that mutation while the patient still looks fine. This approval says: switch drugs at that moment, not at the scan. Doing so roughly doubled the time before the cancer progressed.
items.why: It establishes a regulatory precedent that a molecular signal in blood, with no visible disease change, is enough to approve switching therapy - a template other cancers will follow.

items.headline: US envoys meet Putin for three hours in Moscow, then head to Kyiv
items.body: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin on Saturday for three hours and ten minutes, followed by dinner, in the first substantive US-Russia session after roughly eight months of frozen talks. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov called the discussion "substantive, constructive, exceptionally candid, and conducted in a spirit of trust." Trump said the envoys carried "a proposal to end the war" and that "there may be a good chance we will do it." The envoys were due in Kyiv on Sunday; both sides agreed to a short pause in airstrikes to allow the trip. The central dispute is unchanged: the US framework would have Ukraine cede the remainder of the Donbas in exchange for security guarantees, and Zelensky has repeatedly refused territorial concessions.
items.plain: The Donbas is the industrial region in eastern Ukraine that Russia has been fighting for since 2014; it holds most of Luhansk and about 70% of Donetsk already. The American plan asks Ukraine to hand over the part Russia has not taken, in return for a promise of protection. Ukraine's objection is not sentimental - that territory contains its fortified defensive line, so giving it up means surrendering the ground it would need to stop a future invasion. The airstrike pause is a goodwill gesture, not a ceasefire.
items.why: Both sides agreeing to stop shooting for a few days to let negotiators travel is the first physical concession either has made this year, however small.

items.headline: OpenAI rates its new model Critical for cyber capability, and its benchmark claim is disputed
items.body: GPT-6 Astra, released September 3, is the first model OpenAI has classified as Critical for cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework - its designation for autonomous discovery and exploitation of previously unknown vulnerabilities. During testing the model found two zero-day flaws and chained them into a working exploit; OpenAI says it is disclosing both to maintainers. The released version is restricted to secure code review and patching and refuses proof-of-concept exploit requests. Enterprise customers in OpenAI's Daybreak cyber program got access first, ahead of paying ChatGPT subscribers. Altman apologized on September 4: "first, sorry for the messy rollout. second, when we screw up, we try to make it right." OpenAI reported 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3 using a Provider Adapter harness; ARC Prize, which maintains the benchmark, reported 62.7% under its standard harness.
items.plain: A zero-day is a security hole nobody has patched because nobody knew it existed - the most valuable thing in hacking. OpenAI is saying its model can now find these on its own in real, hardened software and write code to break in, which is why it shipped a version deliberately crippled to only fix code, not attack it. The benchmark fight is a separate matter: OpenAI's headline score used its own testing setup, and the group that built the test got a far lower number using theirs. Both figures are public, so treat the gap as a measurement dispute rather than a settled claim.
items.why: A capability rated dangerous enough to restrict at launch still exists inside the model, and the restriction is a policy choice that competitors under less scrutiny may not copy.

items.headline: First treatment ever approved for Alexander disease
items.body: The FDA approved Zanvastro (zilganersen) from Ionis Pharmaceuticals on September 3 for children and adults with Alexander disease, an ultra-rare, progressive and frequently fatal neurological disorder that damages motor, cognitive, autonomic and gastrointestinal function. It is the first disease-modifying treatment for the condition; until now care was limited to managing symptoms. The drug is an antisense oligonucleotide that reduces production of the abnormal GFAP protein whose accumulation drives the disease, and is given as an injection into the spinal canal once every three months by a trained clinician. Ionis says it will reach US patients within weeks. Recordati holds rights outside the US under a June 2026 license.
items.plain: Alexander disease is caused by a mutation that makes brain support cells produce a faulty version of a structural protein called GFAP, which then piles up and destroys the cells around it. Existing care could only soften the symptoms while that continued. This drug works one step earlier: it is a short strand of synthetic genetic material that binds the instructions for making GFAP and stops them being read, so less of the protein gets built in the first place. It has to be injected into the spinal fluid because drugs in the bloodstream cannot reach the brain.
items.why: Antisense drugs are now clearing approval for diseases with patient populations in the hundreds, which changes the arithmetic of whether ultra-rare conditions are worth developing for at all.

items.headline: Justice Department tells a federal court that training AI on copyrighted work is fair use
items.body: The DOJ filed a statement of interest on September 1 with Judge Sidney Stein in the Southern District of New York, in the consolidated copyright litigation that includes The New York Times' suit against OpenAI and Microsoft. It argues that training large language models on copyrighted text is "extraordinarily transformative" and therefore fair use, separating the training question from claims about model outputs and how data was acquired. The filing says mandatory licensing would threaten national security and create an AI oligopoly favoring the wealthiest developers and legacy outlets with the largest archives, and calls the plaintiffs' market-dilution theory "deeply flawed." The Times responded that "the Administration is siding with a handful of trillion-dollar AI companies at the expense of the countless American creators whose work they stole." A statement of interest is not binding; Stein decides.
items.plain: Fair use is the rule that lets you copy someone's work without permission if you are doing something meaningfully different with it - quoting, parodying, analyzing. Publishers argue that feeding millions of their articles into a model is straightforward copying at scale. A statement of interest is a way for the federal government to tell a judge its view of a case it is not part of. This is the first time it has done so in any of the AI copyright suits, and it landed on the AI companies' side while the case is heading into the decisive phase.
items.why: If Stein adopts the reasoning, the largest financial risk hanging over every frontier AI developer - retroactive licensing liability for training data - mostly disappears.

items.headline: FBI investigates a dark-web service that offered scans of 153 million driver's licenses
items.body: A service called Nexus, advertised on the Russian-language Exploit cybercrime forum, offered digital scans of more than 153 million US and Canadian driver's licenses, over 10 million ID cards, more than 3 million travel documents and roughly 580,000 medical cards. Brian Krebs reported it on September 1 after finding his own license in the collection, and traced the material to IDScan.net, an identity-verification vendor. The FBI's New Orleans field office has opened an investigation and told TIME it is "looking into the incident" but declined further comment. IDScan.net said it is "working urgently to validate that information and determine whether any unauthorized access occurred," adding that it has "not reached conclusions regarding the nature or scope of the incident." Nexus went offline shortly after the report.
items.plain: When a bar, a bank or a rental app scans your license to check you are real, that image usually goes to a third-party verification company you have never heard of. IDScan.net is one of those. A scan is far worse to lose than a password: it is a photograph of a government document with your face, address and birth date, which is exactly what is needed to open accounts in your name, and unlike a password you cannot change it. Note that IDScan.net has not confirmed a breach - the link to it comes from Krebs's analysis of the data.
items.why: The identity-verification industry built to stop fraud has become a single point of failure that concentrates unchangeable credentials for hundreds of millions of people.

items.headline: Judge restricts work on Trump's $100 million arch, days after the Chief Justice called his ballroom likely unlawful
items.body: On Friday, September 4, US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ordered the administration to give the court at least 48 hours' notice before doing anything at the site of Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch except digging pits to identify underground cultural artifacts. The Interior Department had said Thursday it would begin work soon, despite the National Capital Planning Commission having granted only preliminary approval. The plaintiffs - three military veterans and an architectural historian - wrote that the administration has "no legal basis for the construction work" and that the arch requires congressional authorization. Their filing cited the White House ballroom as a "cautionary tale": construction there continued after a district court found it unlawful and the D.C. Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court let the ballroom proceed 5-4 on standing grounds; Chief Justice John Roberts dissented, joined by Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson, writing that the project is "likely unlawful" because Congress has not authorized it. The arch, estimated at $100 million, would stand at the Virginia end of Memorial Bridge near Arlington National Cemetery. Trump has said it should be "the biggest one of all," and said it could be funded from leftover private donations raised for the $400 million ballroom; public money is being used for both.
items.plain: A triumphal arch is the monument a ruler builds to commemorate a military victory - the Arc de Triomphe is the famous one. This would be taller than any in another capital city, at 250 feet. Under the Constitution, Congress controls federal spending and has to authorize permanent construction like this; it has not. The plaintiffs' argument is that the administration learned from the ballroom that it can simply build first, because a half-finished structure is hard for a court to undo. The notable part is who said the ballroom was probably illegal: the Chief Justice, in dissent from his own conservative majority.
items.why: The pattern the veterans describe - build while the case is pending, because concrete is harder to reverse than an order - is now being contested in advance rather than after the fact.
